titulo.texto: Anthropomorphic Sculpture in the Mezcala Style

frase_gancho.texto: A body reduced to its essence: green stone, straight lines and nothing more.

puente_narrativo.texto: From art that strips away every last detail, we move on to another stone from Guerrero, covered in color. Look for a small mask with a serious face, made of tiny green, blue and white pieces.

guion_corto.texto: This human figure of green stone comes from the Mezcala River basin, in Guerrero, and was made about two thousand years ago. It stands about twenty-two centimeters tall, and its body is almost a rectangle. Look at the face: two planes form the brow and the triangular nose, and two horizontal lines are the eyes and the mouth. The arms are two thin lines across the abdomen. There are no details of clothing or adornment, only the essential. The artists of Mezcala did not copy the human body: they distilled it. To make it, they wore the stone down with cords, sand and water, again and again. That is why the surface is so smooth. It looks like modern art, but it is about two thousand years old.

guion_largo.texto:
Many visitors say it when they see it: “this looks like modern art.” And they are right that it is surprising. But what you see is two thousand years old, and it was made with sand, cord and patience.

The artists of Mezcala cut the stone with a thread of plant fiber, wet and covered in sand, pulled taut and drawn back and forth like a saw. Then they wore down the surfaces with sand and water for days. The cuts were straight, the planes clean. They removed everything that was left over, until only the essence of the figure remained. Someone who carves like this is in no hurry.

The stone was hard and green, taken from the canyons of the Balsas River, in Guerrero: serpentine, diorite and others. For the peoples of Mesoamerica, green stone was water, life and young maize. You have already seen it in the [Lord of Las Limas](mna_s08_senor_las_limas), in the Olmec axes and in the [mask of Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal). Here the material is not covered with ornament: it is allowed to speak.

The artists of Mezcala also made small models of temples with columns, flat masks and animals. But the most famous works are human figures like this one, standing or with their arms across the abdomen. Always with that economy of line.

We do not know who they were. The Mezcala culture is known almost only through its stones, and how they lived and what they believed is a mystery. Nor do we know for certain what the figures were for: it has been thought that they were amulets, funerary offerings or images of ancestors. But their art circulated widely: Mezcala pieces have been found in distant places in Guerrero.

And here is an astonishing fact. The Mexica collected these figures. In the offerings of the Templo Mayor, numerous Mezcala pieces have been found, from several centuries before their time, buried together with Olmec objects, like the [axe](mna_s08_hacha_votiva_jade) you saw. For the Mexica they were relics of a remote past. When you look at it, you do the same as they did: you contemplate the antiquity of others.

Walk around the display case and look at it in profile: from the front it has presence, but from the side it is a slab about four centimeters thick. The whole face fits on one plane, and even so it is recognizable.

In the twentieth century, artists such as Diego Rivera and Miguel Covarrubias were fascinated by these pieces and put together collections. Rivera built the Anahuacalli museum, in Coyoacán, to house his. And indeed, their style, with its pure lines, is in dialogue with modern art; some compare them to the sculptures of Constantin Brancusi, a Romanian sculptor of the early twentieth century, although none of this was made with the future in mind.

One final warning. Precisely because it is so highly prized, the Mezcala style is among the most imitated by forgers. That is why a museum piece, with its documented history, is worth so much: it is the one we know to be genuine.

This figure asks a question without words: what do we really need in order to recognize a person? Here a triangle and two lines are enough.

texto: Find the two planes that form the brow and the nose
Look at the horizontal lines of the eyes and the mouth
Run your eyes over the surface: can you see any cut or scratch?

texto.Period: Late Preclassic to Classic (400 BC-600 AD)
texto.Material: Hard stones (mainly green serpentine, metasedimentary rock, and jadeite)

texto.pregunta: Myth: Simple sculptures are primitive works, made by someone who did not know how to do more.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The simplicity of Mezcala was a choice. The artists had mastered the stone and removed everything that was left over.
